title: Chunk-Size and Heap Explorer
description: A 5-second recording is 128,000 bytes in 16-bit form, so how it is sent matters on a Pico. Joining the header and the body copies the whole recording into a second block; sending memoryview slices of K bytes needs only the recording plus a small staging area; and streaming each 1,024-byte frame needs no recording at all.
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Open Study Buddy
Streaming Speech, Security, and Network Resilience
Chunked Audio Upload
Audio Chunk Size
Free Heap
memoryview Slice

learningObjectives: The learner will examine 8 upload designs to decide whether each fits in a given free heap and, for those that fit, how many sends it needs, with at least 7 of 8 correct.
prerequisites: 16-bit and 32-bit recording sizes, memoryview slice, chunk, free heap, contiguous block (all defined in this chapter above this block and in Chapter 2).

accessibility.notes: describe() provides a screen-reader description; all controls are native HTML elements.

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Explore, then fixed-order practice items with one attempt each and immediate explained feedback
keyQuestions: Does sending in chunks make the recording smaller?
Why is joining the header and the body costly?
Why does design D fit at any length of speech?
commonMisconceptions: (1) Sending in chunks makes the recording itself smaller. (2) Joining the header and body is harmless because the recording is already in memory. (3) A bigger free heap total always means a big block is available. (4) Streaming needs the whole recording in memory.
assessmentOpportunities: Complete all eight cases. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.
